newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: North and South Korea in defection crisis.
newsitem.headline: North and South Korea in defection crisis.

text.p: South Korea on Thursday called North Korea's suggestion that Seoul kidnapped one of its top official "preposterous" and said it would step up diplomatic efforts to grant his wish for asylum in the South.

"This is a preposterous claim," said a National Unification ministry spokesman Kang Ho-yang told Reuters the day after Hwang Jang-yop, a senior aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il sought refuge in Seoul's Beijing embassy.
"But such an absurd reaction by the North does not come as a surprise as that has been their usual tactic," the spokesman added.

As a diplomatic crisis erupted over the fate of Hwang, a foreign ministry spokesman said Kim Ha-jung, a special adviser to Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha, left for Beijing on Thursday morning for talks with Chinese officials.

South Korea's foreign ministry said Hwang, one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of Pyongyang's ruling Workers' Party, sought asylum at the embassy on Wednesday with his assistant, Kim Dok-hong.
"We will not spare any effort to honour his wishes," Kang said.
In Beijing, dozens of police sealed off South Korea's consular office where Seoul officials said Hwang was staying.
Lines of police blocked off all approaches to the South Korean embassy's consular section in the diplomtic section of central Beiing.
A Seoul defence ministry official said South Korea's military had heightened vigilance in view of North Korea's "unpredictability".
"The military leadership is carefully analysing the situation and working out possible scenarios to prepare for any contingencies," he said.

Foreign Minister Yoo cancelled a planned trip to Singapore on Wednesday because of Hwang's case but was now considering going there to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, the ministry spokesman said.
Both Yoo and Qian were due to attend a Singapore meeting of officials from Europe and Southeast Asian countries.
Seoul officials said the North would almost certainly pressure Beijing, one of Stalinist North Korea's few allies, not to allow Hwang to head for South Korea.
South Korea said Hwang was the highest ranking Pyongyang official ever to seek asylum in South Korea, and analysts said his defection indicated cracks in the Stalinist hierarchy.
Hwang, 73, is in charge of the North Korean communist party's foreign policy and a member of its central committee, according to Seoul officials, who rank him 24th in the Pyongyang power structure,
Hwang played a leading role in shaping the policy of Juche, a brand of fanatic self-reliance providing the ideological underpinning for the world's last Stalinist state.
Hours after Seoul announced his intention to defect, North Korea said it was inconceivable Hwang was seeking asylum and declared he must have been kidnapped.

A Pyongyang foreign ministry statement issued by the official Korean Central News Agency threatened unspecified countermeasures against South Korea, and called on China to take "appropriate measures".
The defection row broke four days before the much-heralded 55th birthday of Kim, son of the late president Kim Il-sung, who built a personality cult around the Juche creed.
Despite the crisis, South Korea said it would respond to a World Food Programme appeal for $41.6 million in new food aid for North Korea.
The United States said it would join the appeal by the U.N.'s food aid agency to raise 100,000 metric tonnes of aid.

"We haven't been officially notified yet but our position is that we will participate and we will do our share," said an official with Seoul's National Unification Ministry, who declined to be identified.

"North Korea's attitude is the most important thing. There is a possibility that North Korea will counter strongly. We are examining the situation attentively," the official said, referring to the defection wrangle.
Food aid has often been held hostage to political crises between the communist North and the capitalist South.
